# Sources {#sec-sources .unnumbered .pdf-full}

Every prayer text in this book is taken from Wikipedia and is reused under
[CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). The
commentary around the texts is written for this book, from the material in
those same articles.

## Editorial notes

The texts are reproduced as the articles give them, with these exceptions.

**Modern Greek.** The Greek Wikipedia prints its demotic translation in
polytonic orthography with the translator's glosses in parentheses inside the
lines. It appears here in monotonic orthography with the glosses removed, and
with three forms normalised to standard modern spelling — *ἐπιτρέψῃς* →
επιτρέψεις, *ὑποκύψωμε* → υποκύψουμε, *δύναμι* → δύναμη. The article's own
text, for reference:

> Οὐράνιε πατέρα μας, νὰ δοξάζεται τὸ ὄνομά σου, νὰ ἔρχεται ἡ βασιλεία σου (νὰ
> βασιλεύῃς σὲ μᾶς, νὰ κυβερνᾷς τὴ ζωή μας), νὰ γίνεται τὸ θέλημά σου, ὅπως
> στὸν οὐρανό, ἔτσι καὶ στὴ γῆ· τὸ ψωμί μας τὸ ἀναγκαῖο γιὰ τὴ ζωὴ δῶσε μας
> σήμερα καὶ χάρισέ μας τὰ χρέη μας (τὰ ἁμαρτήματά μας), ὅπως καὶ ἐμεῖς
> χαρίζουμε στοὺς χρεῶστες μας (σ᾽ ὅσους ἁμάρτησαν σὲ μᾶς). Καὶ νὰ μὴν
> ἐπιτρέψῃς νὰ ὑποκύψωμε σὲ πειρασμό, ἀλλὰ γλύτωσέ μας ἀπὸ τὸν Πονηρό. Διότι
> δική σου (καὶ ὄχι τοῦ Πονηροῦ) εἶναι ἡ βασιλικὴ ἐξουσία καὶ ἡ δύναμι καὶ ἡ
> ἰσχὺς στοὺς αἰῶνες. Ἀμήν.

**Ukrainian transliteration.** Written for this book, romanising the sound
rather than the spelling. It is not the Ukrainian National system used for
passports and place names, which writes *г* as `h` but also collapses *и* and
*і* in ways that hide the difference between them. The scheme used is set out
in the pronunciation key in that chapter.

**Ukrainian second text.** Ohiyenko's Matthew is quoted from the gospel
comparison table in the same article, which prints it verse by verse; the
verse numbers have been dropped and the text broken at the petitions.

**Modern Greek transliteration.** Written for this book. The Greek Wikipedia
article does not romanise its text, and no standard romanisation targets Modern
Greek *pronunciation* rather than spelling. The scheme used is set out in the
pronunciation key in that chapter.

**Ancient Greek transliteration.** Wikipedia's own, taken from the article
verbatim for both the NA28 and the Patriarchal 1904 texts. The two differ
slightly in how they mark accents, because the article transliterates them in
two separate sections; that inconsistency is preserved rather than smoothed
over.

**German ecumenical text.** The *Vaterunser* article describes the 1968
ecumenical text rather than printing it, saying it matches the 1984 Luther
Bible word for word apart from the inverted address *Vater unser*. The text
given here is quoted verbatim from a different German Wikipedia article,
[Prägermanisch](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pr%C3%A4germanisch), which
prints it in full as its modern-German reference text; it agrees with every
detail the *Vaterunser* article specifies.

**Italian pre-2020 wording.** The chapter quotes the older sixth petition,
*e non ci indurre in tentazione*, from the Italian article's own footnote on
what the 2020 Missal changed. Only the 2020 and Waldensian texts are given as
full prayer blocks, both verbatim.

**Spanish liturgical text.** Assembled from the wording the Spanish article
gives for the current liturgical form, which the article presents split across
a table of the prayer's parts rather than as one continuous block.

**Line breaks.** Where an article runs the prayer as continuous prose, it has
been broken into lines at the petitions. The words are unchanged.

## Audio

The one recording the book plays is from Wikimedia Commons, converted to MP3
at its original sample rate, high-pass filtered at 70 Hz and peak-normalised;
the audio is otherwise unedited.

| Recording | Author | Licence |
|---|---|---|
| [Pater-Noster.ogg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pater-Noster.ogg) — spoken | Dan Palraz | [CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) |

Commons holds two other readings of the prayer in Latin. The one used here was
picked on measurement rather than taste: it has roughly 15 dB more signal
above its noise floor than the next best, which is the difference between a
clean voice and a hissy one. The Gregorian setting sung by [Schola
Gregoriana](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Schola_Gregoriana-Pater_Noster.ogg)
([CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)) still ships
with the site, but each prayer is now offered with a single reading and the
chant is not it.

Commons has no recording of this prayer in Lithuanian, Italian, German or
either form of Greek, so those chapters are read by a voice installed on your
own device — one voice, chosen by the page. Spanish is not read aloud at all.
MIDI files of *Pater noster* and *Vater unser* do exist on Commons, but MIDI
stores notes rather than words — it can carry the chant's melody and never the
text — so it is no use for reading a prayer aloud.

The recording carries a cue list, so it follows the text line by line, as the
chapters read by a voice do. The times were measured rather than estimated:
silence detection finds eight pauses in the reading, exactly the number of
boundaries nine lines need, and each is stable across detection thresholds.
Only the first — a short breath at 3.08s, between *cælis* and *sanctificétur*
— needs a loose threshold to appear at all.

**Ancient Greek, spoken.** The Greek chapters are read by a Modern Greek
voice, which is the Orthodox practice: the Koine text is chanted in Greece
today with modern phonology, not a reconstructed ancient one. But such a voice
knows only monotonic orthography, and drops a word-initial vowel that carries
a breathing mark — it reads *ἁγιασθήτω* as "γιασθήτω" and *ἡμῶν* as "μῶν".
Seventeen of the twenty-one such words in the critical text lost their first
letter. So the chapter keeps polytonic on the page and hands the synthesiser
the same words in monotonic orthography. Two long petitions also take a comma
for phrasing, borrowed from where the 1904 edition punctuates them. No word is
changed.

**Ecclesiastical Latin.** The Latin chapter keeps a respelling of the text —
*cælis* → *célis*, *tentatiónem* → *tentaziónem* — so that an Italian voice
asked to read it produces the ecclesiastical pronunciation; the recording is
played in preference to it. Only the spelling is changed and only for the
synthesiser; the text on the page and in the PDF is the Missal's, untouched.
